categories: ["Postpartum and Breastfeeding", "สภาพเต้านม"]
synonyms: ["Dense Breast Milk", "Dense Milk", "Viscous Breast Milk", "Thick or Discoloured Breast Milk"]
conventional_description:
In conventional Western medicine, thick breast milk is usually considered a variation of normal milk composition or a sign of a plugged milk duct. Breast milk naturally separates into a thinner foremilk and a thicker, fattier hindmilk; sometimes the hindmilk can appear unusually dense or sticky. Other contributing factors include dehydration, infrequent feeding or pumping, and a high intake of saturated fats.
When accompanied by pain, redness, or a palpable lump, thick milk may indicate a blocked duct or early mastitis. Diagnosis is based on clinical history and breast examination, and sometimes a milk culture if infection is suspected. It is not typically treated as a standalone diagnosis but rather as a symptom managed through breastfeeding technique and lifestyle adjustments.
conventional_treatments: Standard advice includes frequent and complete breast emptying, warm compresses before feeding, gentle massage toward the nipple, and ensuring proper latch. Some lactation consultants recommend lecithin supplements to reduce milk viscosity and prevent recurrent plugged ducts. If a bacterial infection develops, antibiotics may be prescribed. Pain relief is managed with over-the-counter anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen.
tcm_understanding:
In Chinese medicine, breast milk is seen as a transformation of Qi and Blood, produced by the body's finest essence. Its quality-texture, color, flow-is a direct mirror of the mother's internal balance, particularly the state of her Liver, Spleen, and Stomach. When these organ systems function smoothly, milk flows freely and is neither too thick nor too thin. When they are disrupted, the milk changes: it can become dense, sticky, clumpy, or difficult to express.
The Liver is responsible for the smooth movement of Qi throughout the body, including the breast channels. Emotional stress, frustration, or unexpressed anger can cause Liver Qi to stagnate, blocking the flow of milk and making it thick and hard to release. The Spleen transforms food and fluids into Qi and Blood; if it is weakened by poor diet, overwork, or constitutional tendency, it fails to manage moisture, and dampness accumulates. This dampness congeals the milk, leaving it viscous and gluey.
The Stomach channel passes directly through the breasts, so heat in the Stomach can rise and dry out the fluids that make milk, resulting in a thick, yellowish, and sometimes bitter-tasting milk. In some cases, prolonged stagnation generates its own heat, combining the effects of blockage and dryness. And when the body's warming Yang energy is deficient, especially in the Spleen, the milk becomes thick from cold congealing rather than heat drying-this is a less common but important pattern.
Because the same symptom of thick milk can arise from such different roots, TCM doesn't offer a single treatment. Instead, a practitioner differentiates the pattern by looking at the whole picture: the milk's color and taste, breast sensation, emotional state, digestion, energy, tongue coating, and pulse quality. This is why two women with thick breast milk may receive completely different herbal formulas and acupuncture points.
classical_quote: 「乳汁稠厚，乃肝气郁结，乳络不通，宜疏肝理气，通络下乳。」
classical_translation: "Thick breast milk is due to Liver Qi stagnation and blocked breast channels; it is appropriate to soothe the Liver, regulate Qi, and unblock the channels to promote milk flow."

Fu Qing Zhu Nv Ke (Fu Qingzhu's Gynecology)  ,  Chapter on Postpartum Lactation Disorders 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner starts by asking about the milk’s texture, color, and taste, and how the breasts feel during let‑down. They also explore your emotional state, diet, energy levels, and any digestive issues, because the quality of breast milk always reflects the balance of Qi and body fluids.
When emotional stress or frustration is the trigger, the pattern is usually Liver Qi Stagnation. The milk is thick and hard to express, the breasts feel distended and lumpy, and the tongue may have a thin white coating with a wiry pulse. These signs point to Qi getting stuck in the breast channels.
If the milk is very viscous and the person tends to eat rich or greasy foods, Phlegm‑Dampness in the Middle‑Burner is likely. The tongue will have a thick, greasy coating and the pulse feels slippery. The breast may feel full but the milk still flows poorly because dampness congeals the fluids.
When the milk is yellowish, thick, and tastes bitter, Stomach Fire is suspected. The tongue is red with a yellow coat, the pulse is rapid and slippery, and you may notice thirst or bad breath. The heat dries up fluids and thickens the milk.
In Spleen Deficiency with Dampness, the milk can be sticky or clumpy despite a reasonable volume. The person feels tired, has a poor appetite, and shows a pale, swollen tongue with a white greasy coating and a soggy, slow pulse. Here the Spleen is too weak to transform fluids properly.
Long‑standing Liver stagnation that generates heat produces a bitter, thick milk with a red tongue that has little coating and a rapid, wiry pulse. A less common pattern, Spleen Yang Deficiency, leads to scanty, thick milk accompanied by cold limbs, a pale tongue, and a deep, slow pulse.

patterns.why_this_happens:
The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, including the breast channels. When emotional stress, frustration, or unexpressed anger build up, the Liver Qi becomes stuck and fails to move freely. This stagnation traps the Qi in the chest and breasts, causing the milk to thicken and become difficult to express.
As the milk sits in the ducts, it loses its fluid, easy-flowing quality and becomes dense and viscous. The breasts feel distended and tender, and the frustration of not being able to nurse easily often makes the stagnation worse.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly dark body, red or slightly purple sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress directly tightens and traps Liver Qi, which is the root mechanism of this pattern, so calming the mind and relaxing the body are the most effective relievers. Warmth and gentle massage help physically move the stuck Qi and encourage milk to flow, while greasy foods burden the Liver and Spleen, adding to stagnation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Make stress relief a priority - even short walks, deep breathing, or a quiet moment can help Liver Qi move. Keep meals light and avoid greasy, fried, or overly rich foods that can add to stagnation. Gentle breast massage toward the nipple before and during nursing can encourage milk flow.

patterns.why_this_happens: A diet rich in greasy, sweet, or cold foods weakens the Spleen's ability to transform and transport fluids. This leads to an accumulation of dampness and phlegm in the body, which can congeal in the breast channels. The result is breast milk that becomes thick, sticky, and difficult to express, even though the breasts feel heavy and full.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen with teeth marks and a thick, white, greasy coating that looks wet. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and soggy (濡 rú), often slow.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, cold, and dairy-rich foods weaken the Spleen and generate dampness and phlegm, which directly thicken breast milk. Warm, light meals and gentle movement strengthen the Spleen's ability to transform fluids, while warmth and massage move Qi and break up stagnation in the breast channels, helping milk flow more freely.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked meals with plenty of lightly cooked vegetables and whole grains. Avoid dairy, greasy fried foods, cold drinks, and excessive sweets, which create more dampness. Gentle daily movement like walking helps the Spleen transform fluids and can improve milk flow.

patterns.why_this_happens: Excess heat in the Stomach dries up the body's fluids, including the fluids that make breast milk. This leaves the milk thick, sticky, and often yellowish. Because the Stomach channel passes through the breast area, the heat travels upward and directly influences the quality of the milk, sometimes giving it a bitter taste.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly with central prickles, thick dry yellow coat. Pulse: rapid, slippery, and full; especially forceful in the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stomach Fire is an excess heat pattern. Spicy, greasy foods and alcohol add more heat to the body, while anger stirs up fire. These worsen the drying effect on milk. Cooling foods and drinks directly counteract the internal heat, helping to restore fluids and thin the milk. Gentle exercise prevents Qi stagnation, which can generate heat, and stress reduction calms the mind, preventing emotional fire from flaring up.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on cooling, hydrating foods like cucumber, watermelon, pear, and leafy greens. Avoid spicy, fried, or greasy dishes, and cut back on alcohol and coffee. Drink plenty of room-temperature or cool water. Gentle daily movement like walking helps keep Qi flowing and prevents heat from building up.

patterns.why_this_happens:
The Spleen is in charge of transforming and moving body fluids. When Spleen Qi is weak, it cannot properly process those fluids, and a heavy, sticky dampness builds up inside. This dampness seeps into the breast milk, making it feel thick, clumpy, or gluey rather than smooth and free-flowing.
The milk volume may seem adequate, but the dampness makes it hard to express, and the breasts often feel heavy and full without the sharp pain of more inflammatory patterns.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks and a white greasy coating; surface is moist. Pulse: soggy (濡 ru) and slow (缓 huǎn), possibly slippery.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen thrives on warmth and regularity. Cold and raw foods douse its digestive fire, while greasy and sweet foods generate more dampness that thickens the milk. Warmth, rest, and gentle movement support the Spleen's ability to transform fluids, so the milk becomes less sticky and flows more freely.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees. Avoid cold, raw, greasy, and overly sweet foods, which create more dampness. Gentle daily movement like walking helps Qi circulate and dry out dampness. Warm compresses on the breasts before feeding can soften the milk and make it easier to express.

patterns.symptoms: ["Breast milk is thick and may have a bitter taste", "Irritability and explosive anger", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Distending or burning pain in the ribcage", "Red face and eyes", "Dry mouth and throat"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, anger, or frustration, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol and caffeine, Hot or hot-humid weather, Skipping or delaying breastfeeding

patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, including the breast channels. When emotional stress and frustration are prolonged, Liver Qi becomes stuck, and milk cannot flow freely, causing it to stagnate and thicken. Over time, this stagnation generates internal heat, which further thickens the milk and may give it a bitter taste, while also causing the classic signs of heat such as irritability, a red tongue, and a rapid pulse.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, redder at the sides, with a yellow coating. Pulse: wiry and rapid (xian shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and anger are the root cause of Liver Qi stagnation, and they directly worsen the condition. Spicy and greasy foods add heat to the body, which further thickens the milk. Cooling foods and drinks, along with calming activities, help clear heat and move stagnant Qi, allowing milk to flow smoothly again. Regular milk expression prevents stasis and reduces the chance of heat building up.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat cooling, light foods like leafy greens, cucumber, and chrysanthemum tea. Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol, which add heat. Manage stress with gentle exercise like walking or yoga, and ensure you express milk regularly to prevent stasis.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When Spleen Yang is too weak to warm the body, the transformation and transportation of fluids become sluggish and cold. This internal cold thickens the breast milk, making it dense and difficult to flow, while also reducing the overall volume.
The cold nature of this pattern means the milk often feels cool and is scanty, and the mother may feel generally chilled, with cold hands and feet and a deep dislike of cold environments.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tender with scalloped edges and a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Yang Deficiency is a cold, empty condition. Warmth and rest help to preserve and gently restore the body's own warming fire, while cold, raw foods and exhaustion drain what little Yang remains. Warming foods and moxibustion directly supply the heat needed to thin the milk and encourage its flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews. Use ginger, cinnamon, and black pepper generously. Avoid cold, raw, and frozen foods. Keep the abdomen and lower back warm with a hot water bottle. Gentle moxibustion at home over the navel can be very soothing.

faqs.question: Is thick breast milk harmful to my baby?
faqs.answer: In most cases, no. Thick milk is still nutritious, and babies can usually extract it with a strong suck. However, if the milk is excessively sticky or clumpy, it may be harder for the baby to get a full feeding, leading to frustration or poor weight gain. TCM treatment aims to normalize the milk's texture so feeding becomes easier and more satisfying for both of you.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with thick breast milk?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture helps by moving stagnant Qi, resolving dampness, or clearing heat-depending on your pattern. Points on the breast, chest, and along the Stomach and Liver channels are used to directly unblock the milk ducts and restore smooth flow. Many women feel a softening of the breasts and easier let-down after just a few sessions.

faqs.question: Will the herbs I take affect my baby through breast milk?
faqs.answer: When prescribed by a qualified TCM practitioner, herbal formulas for lactation are carefully selected to be safe for the nursing baby. Many herbs have been used for centuries to support breastfeeding. It's important to work with a practitioner who knows which herbs are appropriate during lactation and at what dosage. Always inform your practitioner that you are breastfeeding, and tell your doctor about any herbs you are taking.

faqs.question: How soon will I see improvement?
faqs.answer: Some women notice a difference within a few days, especially if the pattern is one of simple stagnation. For dampness or deficiency patterns, improvement is more gradual-often over several weeks. Your practitioner will track changes in milk texture, breast comfort, and your overall energy to gauge progress and adjust treatment as needed.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a big role in milk quality. In general, TCM recommends avoiding greasy, spicy, and very cold foods, which can create dampness or heat. Warm, cooked meals like soups and stews are best. Your practitioner will give you specific advice based on your pattern-for example, adding ginger and cinnamon if you tend to feel cold, or chrysanthemum tea if you have signs of heat.

faqs.question: Can stress cause thick breast milk?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. In Chinese medicine, emotional stress directly affects the Liver, which governs the smooth flow of Qi. When Liver Qi stagnates, milk can become thick and difficult to express. This is one of the most common patterns we see, and treatment focuses on relieving stress, moving Qi, and calming the mind-alongside local breast care.

research.title: Acupuncture for postpartum insufficient lactation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This systematic review evaluated 12 RCTs and found that acupuncture significantly increased milk volume and reduced breast distension compared to no treatment or conventional care. The most commonly used points were Rugen ST-18, Shanzhong REN-17, and Zusanli ST-36. No serious adverse events were reported.

research.title: Effect of Xia Ru Yong Quan San on breast milk viscosity and flow in postpartum women: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: In this RCT of 120 women with thick, difficult-to-express milk, the herbal group showed a significant reduction in milk viscosity and improvement in breastfeeding comfort after two weeks compared to placebo. Liver Qi Stagnation was the predominant pattern in 70% of participants.
